Below is a synthesis of the evidence on how doctoral programs connect to the productive sector (i.e., industry, firms, and innovation-driven markets), including mechanisms, governance models, measurable outcomes, and remaining challenges.

Conceptual link: from doctoral training to the productive sector
- Doctoral programs contribute to the productive sector by training highly skilled researchers who can bridge academia and industry, translate science into applications, and enhance firms’ R&D and innovation capabilities. Collaborative doctoral education explicitly trains “boundary spanners” who can move between academic and industrial logics, and such programs often yield high industry placement rates and facilitate commercialization via embedded projects and joint supervision. <cite id="d447a93a-0">Collaborative doctoral programs jointly organized by academia and industry facilitate doctoral students’ and graduates’ movement between academia and industry, with a clear majority of participants in such programs continuing to work in industry after graduation; industrial partners value fresh ideas, scientific knowledge, and the ability to employ newly graduated PhDs in internal R&D to commercialize university innovations, thereby increasing firms’ knowledge resources and capabilities</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-4">Doctoral programs are theorized as boundary-spanning mechanisms that amplify university–industry knowledge exchange; doctoral training confers original knowledge creation, methodological rigor, close supervision, and independent thinking that can diffuse deeper analytical and research-based capabilities into organizational contexts</cite>.

Mechanisms of linkage
- Boundary spanning and co-creation: <cite id="d447a93a-0">Industrial actors and academics engaged in collaborative doctoral programs report that students bring innovative mindsets and scientific knowledge into industry, lower the threshold for PhDs to transfer into industrial careers, and build personal networks and trust that overcome organizational and cultural barriers</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-2">Under the Triple Helix model, industrial doctorates are recognized as strategic tools to diversify the role of PhD graduates in the economy, foster cooperation nationally and regionally, and implement regional innovation strategies; governments stimulate collaboration through policies and grants, companies provide grants and training, and universities broaden cross-disciplinary knowledge and transfer skills</cite>.
- Skills alignment and “T-shaped” profiles: <cite id="5cd7938e-1">Studies of Industrial PhDs describe them as effective for enhancing university–industry knowledge transfer and for developing a “T-shaped” profile—broad field-relevant knowledge plus deep specialization—valuable for industry integration</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-2">Hands-on industry experience during doctoral training enhances career preparedness; programs with split time between company and university expose PhDs to commercial environments, IP awareness, leadership, and varied priorities, broadening career options beyond academia</cite>.
- Embedded/in-company PhDs and internships: <cite id="d447a93a-0">Industrial partners value employing PhDs directly in R&D, using doctoral projects to commercialize innovations and to recruit high-skill graduates who can internalize academic knowledge</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-0">Industry internships for full-time PhD students can bridge academia–industry engagement, develop transferable skills, and increase employability; a national internship program in Australia identified competence clusters (PCAP: PhD, contextual, adaptation, project management) that HR and industry can use to evaluate performance and design jobs</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-4">In-company industrial PhDs fully employed by industry while meeting academic demands are documented, with program documentation and interviews used to validate collaboration structures and integration of workplace and research tasks</cite>.
- Dual-sector steering and alignment: <cite id="d447a93a-1">Industrial PhD reforms in Italy require formal agreements with companies, joint project design, training periods within companies, and company representation on steering committees; thematic areas align with digital transformation, sustainability, and advanced manufacturing, with spatial distributions shifting toward regional innovation hotspots</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-3">Industrial doctorates in Italy are framed as strategic assets for connecting academic research with industry needs, with stricter criteria and governance enhancing alignment and partnerships</cite>.

Governance and policy models connecting to industry
- Triple Helix and funding levers: <cite id="d447a93a-2">Industrial doctorates are embedded in Triple Helix policy frameworks where universities, industry, and government co-govern doctoral training; governments mediate interactions, companies provide grants/training, and universities redesign curricula for cross-disciplinary knowledge and transfer skills</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-1">EU funding (FSE/FESR) under Italy’s National Research Plan supported industrial and intersectoral PhDs with company agreements, joint project design, and in-company training periods; 2021 criteria strengthened company involvement and alignment</cite>.
- National exemplars: <cite id="5cd7938e-0">Australia’s national Postgraduate Research Internship program supports industry internships for PhD students, aiming to foster collaboration and practical research environments while mapping competence requirements for industry hiring</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-2">Programs across Australia, Europe, and elsewhere show that partnerships among government, industry, and academia produce teamwork, IP awareness, and leadership skills valued in non-academic work</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-1">Case studies (e.g., Synopsys, the Industrial Doctorate Center at Bristol & Bath, KU Leuven’s semi-industrial PhD) report positive effects on knowledge transfer and T-shaped skill development, while also calling for deeper assessment of barriers in practical application</cite>.
- Dual PhD/MBA and entrepreneurship pathways: <cite id="27fb7af1-0">The UNC Charlotte PAtENT program aligns doctoral STEM training with entrepreneurship via patenting, business/ marketing coursework, and experiential opportunities; early evidence suggests improved alignment with a shifting employment landscape and development of entrepreneurial mindsets</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-0">Collaborative doctoral programs have been shown to motivate students to adopt industry-oriented mindsets and practices, increasing the supply of boundary-spanning talent for firms</cite>.

Evidence on outcomes for the productive sector
- Placement and employment in industry: <cite id="d447a93a-0">In collaborative programs, a clear majority of doctoral participants continue in industry after graduation, supplying firms with high-skill researchers; industrial partners report benefits from fresh ideas and R&D capacity building</cite>. <cite id="27fb7af1-4">Across U.S. fields, engineering PhDs are most likely to enter industry, and placements tend to occur in establishments that are firm-owned, R&D-intensive, high-payroll, young, and growth-oriented—profiles consistent with productive-sector absorption and dynamism</cite>.
- Earnings and productivity-related indicators: <cite id="27fb7af1-4">Industry earnings for PhDs are substantially higher than academic or government employment, with math/computer science and engineering showing mean industry earnings near $80–90k one year post-graduation; placements skew toward high-payroll establishments</cite>. <cite id="27fb7af1-2">In developing contexts like Colombia, increasing the number of PhD holders is argued to institutionalize productive university–industry relationships and raise patents and prototypes, though university patenting remains low on average</cite>.
- Entrepreneurship and patenting pathways: <cite id="27fb7af1-0">Student-centered doctoral programs that integrate patenting and entrepreneurship coursework create pathways to commercialization and align with evolving labor markets</cite>. <cite id="27fb7af1-3">Evidence from inventor mobility shows that granted patents significantly reduce employer switching (by 23% on average), indicating that patent-backed innovation skills become firm-specific capital that supports firm retention and innovation investment</cite>.
- Regional innovation alignment: <cite id="d447a93a-1">Industrial PhD programs’ thematic foci and geographic distribution shift toward regional innovation hotspots, suggesting that doctoral training aligns with local productive structures and fosters regional economic development</cite>.

Public vs. private benefits and developing-country considerations
- Human capital formation and societal returns: <cite id="27fb7af1-1">Despite a declining economic value signal in some countries, PhDs still exhibit high employment rates (~94%) and strong relative earnings; about 32.4% of U.S. PhDs enter industry; many find roles in R&D-intensive firms</cite>. <cite id="27fb7af1-2">In developing countries, scaling PhDs—especially through industrial PhDs—can institutionalize productive university–industry ties and raise applied outputs (e.g., patents, prototypes), but policies must ensure public financing to avoid private-returns capture that undermines broader development goals</cite>.
- Universities as knowledge exchange amplifiers: <cite id="d447a93a-4">Doctoral completions can serve as boundary-spanning conduits for university technology transfer and commercialization, but pathways of diffusion into workplaces remain under-theorized and under-empiricized relative to undergraduate/graduate training</cite>.

Barriers and challenges in linking doctorates to the productive sector
- Skills mismatch and outdated training: <cite id="5cd7938e-0">Despite growing industry transitions, PhDs face outdated training models, skills mismatch, and over-qualification; national internship programs aim to bridge this gap by embedding practical industry experience and competence frameworks</cite>.
- Perception gaps and governance frictions: <cite id="5cd7938e-2">While industry-oriented programs often yield benefits, academic supervisors may perceive limited gains from training in industry settings, suggesting misaligned expectations and incentives</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-1">Scholars note that many studies portray Industrial PhDs positively but call for deeper assessments of barriers and practical challenges; the model is promising but not universally adopted as a panacea</cite>.
- Measuring impact and theorizing pathways: <cite id="d447a93a-4">Although doctoral graduates possess advanced capabilities, empirical evidence on how knowledge diffuses into workplaces and measurable spillovers (e.g., patents, productivity) remains insufficient; more systematic, program-level evaluations are needed</cite>.

Practical design levers for stronger linkages
- Curriculum and co-supervision with industry: <cite id="d447a93a-1">Adopt joint project design, in-company training periods, and formal company representation in steering committees to align topics with sectoral needs and innovation priorities</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-2">Structure split-time or semi-industrial models to expose PhDs to commercialization processes, IP regimes, and firm decision-making, building T-shaped competencies</cite>.
- Internship and preceptorship pathways: <cite id="5cd7938e-0">Use national or institutional internship programs to insert PhDs into industry projects with clear performance metrics and competence frameworks (e.g., PCAP) to improve employability and knowledge transfer</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-4">Document and validate collaboration structures (annual study plans, contact persons) to reduce coordination frictions and clarify academic and workplace expectations</cite>.
- Entrepreneurship and patent education: <cite id="27fb7af1-0">Integrate entrepreneurship coursework, patent clinics, and business strategy into doctoral training to create viable pathways from lab to market</cite>.
- Policy scaffolding: <cite id="d447a93a-2">Align national and regional policies to incentivize Triple Helix doctoral partnerships, mediate academia–industry interactions, and fund dual-sector governance</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-1">Leverage EU-style funding with governance levers (company agreements, steering committees) to target innovation hotspots and strengthen productive-sector linkages</cite>.

What remains uncertain
- Quantifying causal spillovers: While mechanisms and directional indicators (industry placements, higher earnings, mobility effects of patents, and regional alignment) are documented, there is a need for more causal, program-level evidence on increases in firm patents, productivities, and startup formation attributable to doctoral training structures. <cite id="d447a93a-4">The literature calls for more empirical work on how doctoral knowledge diffuses into workplaces and contributes to innovation</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-1">Scholars argue for broader assessment beyond potential benefits to include barriers and conditions under which industrial PhDs fail to deliver at scale</cite>.

Summary: why the link matters for the productive sector
- Doctoral programs can be powerful engines for connecting research to production by cultivating boundary-spanning talent, embedding research in firm contexts, and aligning curricula and governance with industry needs. The evidence shows higher industry placement and earnings for many PhDs, stronger inventor retention via patent-backed human capital, and program designs that target innovation hotspots and commercialization. <cite id="d447a93a-0">Collaborative doctoral education delivers industry-ready researchers who accelerate commercialization and build internal R&D capabilities in firms</cite>. <cite id="27fb7af1-4">Placement and earnings patterns indicate absorption into productive-sector establishments, especially in engineering and computer science</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-1">Industrial PhD models enhance knowledge transfer and skill breadth but require careful governance to overcome practical barriers</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-1">Policy frameworks that mandate alignment with company needs and innovation clusters strengthen these linkages at regional and national levels</cite>.

Implication: Strengthening doctoral programs’ link to the productive sector requires coordinated changes in curriculum, supervision, funding, and evaluation to ensure that the original knowledge and methodological power of doctoral training translate reliably into firm-level innovation, entrepreneurship, and regional economic upgrading. <cite id="d447a93a-2">Under the Triple Helix model, universities, industry, and government must co-design doctoral offerings that produce transferable skills and co-owned knowledge assets</cite>. <cite id="5cd7938e-0">Embedding internships with competence frameworks and clear performance indicators can close skills gaps and accelerate workforce integration</cite>. <cite id="27fb7af1-0">Entrepreneurship and patenting curricula can convert basic research into market value</cite>. <cite id="d447a93a-4">As doctoral completions act as boundary-spanning conduits, systematic measurement and support for their knowledge diffusion into workplaces are essential to realize broader societal and productive-sector benefits</cite>.

Title: Australian doctoral graduates’ career transition from academia to industry: the PCAP internship competence framework
Snippet: Although an increasing number of PhD graduates in economically advanced countries transition to industry work post-graduation (O'Shea and Jungblut 2023), this shift is challenging due to outdated training models (Sharmini and Spronken-Smith 2020), a skills mismatch (De Grande et al. 2014;Muurlink et al. 2024), and perceived over-qualification (Ma et al. 2020). However, there is little understanding of the competences required for effective employment in industry (Muurlink et al. 2024). Based on semi-structured interviews with 26 participants from an Australian PhD internship program, this paper investigates the essential competences needed by PhD graduates for effective industry internships. 

Conceptualising the competences of PhD interns is crucial, as internships provide a valuable bridge for PhD candidates and graduates transitioning into industry. Research internships facilitate academia-industry engagement (Kunttu, Huttu, and Neuvo 2018), and enhance career adaptability (Ocampo et al. 2020), develop transferable skills, and motivate individuals to seek opportunities outside academia (Jones and Warnock 2015). This paper focuses on the Australian Postgraduate Research Intern program, Australia's only national industry internship program dedicated to fostering industry-university collaboration and empowering students in a practical research environment. 

This study contributes to the theoretical literature on doctoral education by introducing the PCAP framework identifying key competences for PhD internships. The acronym PCAP stands for PhD competences, Contextual competences, Adaptation competences, and Project management competences. We argue that PhD interns need to develop these four interactive clusters of competences for successful transition into industry roles. The PCAP framework can be used practically by PhD interns, supervisors, and support staff to identify doctoral internship training needs, while Human Resources (HR) recruiters and industry managers can apply the PCAP when drafting job descriptions and evaluating intern performance, making internships more effective and increasing the industry employability of PhD graduates.

The three doctoral education programs presented in this article show that collaborative programs in doctoral education train both industrial actors and academics through boundary-spanning activities. 

A key finding of this study was that collaborative doctoral education programs jointly organized by academia and industry clearly facilitate and motivate the doctoral students and graduates to cross the border between academia and industry. Title: Australian doctoral graduates’ career transition from academia to industry: the PCAP internship competence framework
Snippet: Although an increasing number of PhD graduates in economically advanced countries transition to industry work post-graduation (O'Shea and Jungblut 2023), this shift is challenging due to outdated training models (Sharmini and Spronken-Smith 2020), a skills mismatch (De Grande et al. 2014;Muurlink et al. 2024), and perceived over-qualification (Ma et al. 2020). Researchers have identified the need to support PhD graduates' career transition to industry (Hancock 2023), one approach being to establish industry internships for full-time PhD students with limited prior work experience (Valencia-Forrester 2019). However, there is little understanding of the competences required for effective employment in industry (Muurlink et al. 2024). Based on semi-structured interviews with 26 participants from an Australian PhD internship program, this paper investigates the essential competences needed by PhD graduates for effective industry internships. 

Conceptualising the competences of PhD interns is crucial, as internships provide a valuable bridge for PhD candidates and graduates transitioning into industry. Research internships facilitate academia-industry engagement (Kunttu, Huttu, and Neuvo 2018), and enhance career adaptability (Ocampo et al. 2020), develop transferable skills, and motivate individuals to seek opportunities outside academia (Jones and Warnock 2015). This paper focuses on the Australian Postgraduate Research Intern program, Australia's only national industry internship program dedicated to fostering industry-university collaboration and empowering students in a practical research environment. 

This study contributes to the theoretical literature on doctoral education by introducing the PCAP framework identifying key competences for PhD internships. The acronym PCAP stands for PhD competences, Contextual competences, Adaptation competences, and Project management competences. We argue that PhD interns need to develop these four interactive clusters of competences for successful transition into industry roles. The PCAP framework can be used practically by PhD interns, supervisors, and support staff to identify doctoral internship training needs, while Human Resources (HR) recruiters and industry managers can apply the PCAP when drafting job descriptions and evaluating intern performance, making internships more effective and increasing the industry employability of PhD graduates.

Title: Assessing the industrial PhD: Stakeholder insights
Snippet: As the awareness for a need of change in engineering education rises, various innovative program concepts have been introduced. Thereby, some scholars have been accessing the model of the Industrial PhD. Among them are works on the examples of a cooperative PhD model employed by Synopsys Inc. (Melikyam et al., 2007), the Industrial Doctorate Center (IDC) as a joint program of University of Bristol and University of Bath (Yearworth, 2011), as well as the model of the semi-industrial PhD program of KU Leuven (Granata & Dochy, 2013) and case studies of Industrial PhDs in the Swedish automotive and pharmaceutical industry (Khilander, Nilsson, Lund, Ritzén & Bergendahl, 2011). 

Most of these studies draw a positive picture of the Industrial PhD and describe it as a potentially effective means not only to enhance the transfer of knowledge between universities and industry (Heldal, Söderström, Bråthe & Murby, 2014;Khilander et al., 2011), but also to help PhD students develop a "T-shaped" skill profile (Borrell-Damian, Brown, Dearing, Font, Hagen, Metcalfe et al., 2010), which combines a broad field-relevant knowledge with an in-depth expertise in a specialized area. 

The existing studies, however, circle around the question whether the I.PhD has the potential to become an appropriate solution to the challenge of increasing pressure for change in the education of engineering PhD students. A deeper assessment of the experience academia and industry stakeholders made with I.PhD programs allows insight into whether or not this model offers a proper solution to this challenge and into the barriers threatening the success of this model in its practical application.

Title: PhD graduates pursuing careers beyond academia: a scoping review
Snippet: This second research focus (n = 6) reflects a growing interest in programme-level initiatives aimed at strengthening PhDs' connections to non-academic employment through structured collaboration with industry. This literature body highlights how hands-on industry experience during doctoral training enhances career preparedness. 

Industry-oriented programmes often involve partnerships in which PhD students split their time between a company and university, with both institutions contributing resources and supervision to the project. Such collaborations expose PhDs to both academic and commercial environments, expanding their career options. Manathunga et al. studied Australian PhD programmes promoting collaboration among government, industry, and academia, finding that PhDs gained teamwork, intellectual property awareness, and leadership skills -all valuable in non-academic contexts. In Europe, Borrell-Damian et al. highlighted industry-oriented programmes' benefits, such as exposing PhDs to varied work environments and priorities. Similarly, Lee and Miozzo noted that industry-based PhD projects enhance socialisation into industry cultures, providing an advantage for PhDs entering the private sector. Conversely, Grimm examined an industry-oriented PhD programme in Germany and found that academic thesis supervisors, unlike industry representatives, perceived limited benefits from training PhDs in industry settings.

Title: Shaping Innovation: A Regional Perspective on Industrial PhD Programs in Italy
Snippet: Doctoral education has evolved into a strategic asset for connecting academic research with industry
needs. Industrial PhDs promote collaboration between universities and the private sector, aligning
with the Triple Helix model of interaction among academia, industry, and government. In Italy,
reforms under the National Research Plan 2015–2020 and Ministerial Decree n. 45/2013 introduced
innovative doctoral programs, including industrial and intersectoral PhDs, emphasizing integration
with non-academic sectors. These programs benefit from EU FSE/FESR funding, requiring formal
agreements with companies, joint project design, and training periods within companies or abroad. In
2021, stricter criteria for Industrial PhDs mandated specific scientific projects and company
representation in Steering Committees, enhancing their alignment with industry needs. This study
examines Industrial PhD programs in 2022–2023, using text analysis (LDA) on program titles to
identify thematic areas like digital transformation, sustainability, and advanced manufacturing.
Spatial analysis explores the relationship between program distribution and regional innovation
performance.
Preliminary findings suggest a growing alignment of Industrial PhDs with innovation hotspots, as
evidenced by changes in spatial distribution and program focus. This indicates strategic
diversification, influenced by funding policies and strengthened academia-industry partnerships,
fostering innovation and regional economic development.

Title: University-Industry Collaboration in Higher Education: Exploring the Informing Flows Framework in Industrial PhD Education
Snippet: This study explores the informing flows framework on university-industry collaboration in higher education with focus on industrial PhD education in order to capture the perspectives of industrial PhD students and of industry. A qualitative methodology was applied, and individual semi-structured interviews were conducted in two steps to reveal (i) industrial PhD students' views on the PhD program and collaboration between research, university, and industry in autumn 2019, and (ii) industry's' views on investing in industrial PhD education and interaction between research, university, and industry in spring 2020. Furthermore, document studies were conducted as data was collected via the university administration from the industrial PhD-students' official annual individual study plans for the PhD study programs in order to validate information about the PhD students, their employment, their study progress, their thesis project and scientific work, and contact persons at their organizations. Hence, in this qualitative, interpretive study, we aimed at striving for research rigor by selection of respondents, semi-structured and coded interviews, use of respondent validation and triangulation to confirm findings, and awareness of how to reduce researched bias (Gill & Gill, 2020). Furthermore, a detailed documentation of all steps in the research process was conducted in order to enhance transparency replicability. 

During 2020 the School of Business, Economics and IT, University West had five enrolled industrial PhD students and nine traditional academic PhD students within the field of informatics with a specialization in WIL. documents.title: Australian doctoral graduates’ career transition from academia to industry: the PCAP internship competence framework
documents.snippet:
Although an increasing number of PhD graduates in economically advanced countries transition to industry work post-graduation (O'Shea and Jungblut 2023), this shift is challenging due to outdated training models (Sharmini and Spronken-Smith 2020), a skills mismatch (De Grande et al. 2014;Muurlink et al. 2024), and perceived over-qualification (Ma et al. 2020). Researchers have identified the need to support PhD graduates' career transition to industry (Hancock 2023), one approach being to establish industry internships for full-time PhD students with limited prior work experience (Valencia-Forrester 2019). However, there is little understanding of the competences required for effective employment in industry (Muurlink et al. 2024). Based on semi-structured interviews with 26 participants from an Australian PhD internship program, this paper investigates the essential competences needed by PhD graduates for effective industry internships. 

Conceptualising the competences of PhD interns is crucial, as internships provide a valuable bridge for PhD candidates and graduates transitioning into industry. Research internships facilitate academia-industry engagement (Kunttu, Huttu, and Neuvo 2018), and enhance career adaptability (Ocampo et al. 2020), develop transferable skills, and motivate individuals to seek opportunities outside academia (Jones and Warnock 2015). This paper focuses on the Australian Postgraduate Research Intern program, Australia's only national industry internship program dedicated to fostering industry-university collaboration and empowering students in a practical research environment. 

This study contributes to the theoretical literature on doctoral education by introducing the PCAP framework identifying key competences for PhD internships. The acronym PCAP stands for PhD competences, Contextual competences, Adaptation competences, and Project management competences. We argue that PhD interns need to develop these four interactive clusters of competences for successful transition into industry roles. The PCAP framework can be used practically by PhD interns, supervisors, and support staff to identify doctoral internship training needs, while Human Resources (HR) recruiters and industry managers can apply the PCAP when drafting job descriptions and evaluating intern performance, making internships more effective and increasing the industry employability of PhD graduates.

documents.title: Assessing the industrial PhD: Stakeholder insights
documents.snippet:
As the awareness for a need of change in engineering education rises, various innovative program concepts have been introduced. Thereby, some scholars have been accessing the model of the Industrial PhD. Among them are works on the examples of a cooperative PhD model employed by Synopsys Inc. (Melikyam et al., 2007), the Industrial Doctorate Center (IDC) as a joint program of University of Bristol and University of Bath (Yearworth, 2011), as well as the model of the semi-industrial PhD program of KU Leuven (Granata & Dochy, 2013) and case studies of Industrial PhDs in the Swedish automotive and pharmaceutical industry (Khilander, Nilsson, Lund, Ritzén & Bergendahl, 2011). 

Most of these studies draw a positive picture of the Industrial PhD and describe it as a potentially effective means not only to enhance the transfer of knowledge between universities and industry (Heldal, Söderström, Bråthe & Murby, 2014;Khilander et al., 2011), but also to help PhD students develop a "T-shaped" skill profile (Borrell-Damian, Brown, Dearing, Font, Hagen, Metcalfe et al., 2010), which combines a broad field-relevant knowledge with an in-depth expertise in a specialized area. 

The existing studies, however, circle around the question whether the I.PhD has the potential to become an appropriate solution to the challenge of increasing pressure for change in the education of engineering PhD students. A deeper assessment of the experience academia and industry stakeholders made with I.PhD programs allows insight into whether or not this model offers a proper solution to this challenge and into the barriers threatening the success of this model in its practical application.

documents.title: PhD graduates pursuing careers beyond academia: a scoping review
documents.snippet:
This second research focus (n = 6) reflects a growing interest in programme-level initiatives aimed at strengthening PhDs' connections to non-academic employment through structured collaboration with industry. This literature body highlights how hands-on industry experience during doctoral training enhances career preparedness. 

Industry-oriented programmes often involve partnerships in which PhD students split their time between a company and university, with both institutions contributing resources and supervision to the project. Such collaborations expose PhDs to both academic and commercial environments, expanding their career options. Manathunga et al. studied Australian PhD programmes promoting collaboration among government, industry, and academia, finding that PhDs gained teamwork, intellectual property awareness, and leadership skills -all valuable in non-academic contexts. In Europe, Borrell-Damian et al. highlighted industry-oriented programmes' benefits, such as exposing PhDs to varied work environments and priorities. Similarly, Lee and Miozzo noted that industry-based PhD projects enhance socialisation into industry cultures, providing an advantage for PhDs entering the private sector. Conversely, Grimm examined an industry-oriented PhD programme in Germany and found that academic thesis supervisors, unlike industry representatives, perceived limited benefits from training PhDs in industry settings.

documents.title: Shaping Innovation: A Regional Perspective on Industrial PhD Programs in Italy
documents.snippet:
Doctoral education has evolved into a strategic asset for connecting academic research with industry
needs. Industrial PhDs promote collaboration between universities and the private sector, aligning
with the Triple Helix model of interaction among academia, industry, and government. In Italy,
reforms under the National Research Plan 2015–2020 and Ministerial Decree n. 45/2013 introduced
innovative doctoral programs, including industrial and intersectoral PhDs, emphasizing integration
with non-academic sectors. These programs benefit from EU FSE/FESR funding, requiring formal
agreements with companies, joint project design, and training periods within companies or abroad. In
2021, stricter criteria for Industrial PhDs mandated specific scientific projects and company
representation in Steering Committees, enhancing their alignment with industry needs. This study
examines Industrial PhD programs in 2022–2023, using text analysis (LDA) on program titles to
identify thematic areas like digital transformation, sustainability, and advanced manufacturing.
Spatial analysis explores the relationship between program distribution and regional innovation
performance.
Preliminary findings suggest a growing alignment of Industrial PhDs with innovation hotspots, as
evidenced by changes in spatial distribution and program focus. This indicates strategic
diversification, influenced by funding policies and strengthened academia-industry partnerships,
fostering innovation and regional economic development.

Summary
Shortening doctoral programs to three years can strengthen links to the productive sector if the acceleration is paired with intensified, work-integrated training, industrial co-supervision, and sponsorship, but it can also weaken those links if it compresses breadth, mentoring, and time for alignment with employer needs without compensating resources and assessment standards. The balance depends on redesign—not just duration—so that the degree remains recognized by employers and universities while producing earlier entry-to-practice, richer internships/collaborations, and clearer career scaffolding for non-academic roles. <cite id="a5e35afd-0">Recent reviews emphasize that doctoral education must better align with labor-market realities and support diverse sectoral careers, especially beyond academia</cite> <cite id="a5e35afd-3">as tenure-track and federal research roles have shrunk, programs have been called out to systematically prepare students for industry, government, and national labs</cite> <cite id="198a4bb2-3">and industrial doctorates are reshaping knowledge flows across university–industry–government interfaces</cite>.

How a 3-year model changes mechanisms of linkage
- Time to practice and market responsiveness. Reducing time-to-degree lowers the interval between skill formation and first job search, enabling earlier entry in industry and faster feedback into curricula. <cite id="a5e35afd-3">Cross-discipline evidence shows many master’s and doctoral recipients work in industry and government, underscoring the value of training that maps to these roles</cite>. <cite id="198a4bb2-0">In UK CASE (Collaborative Award) industrial PhDs, co-supervision by an industry mentor alongside an academic supervisor is associated with higher employability and broader skills</cite>. These models compress the bridge between study and work via embedded industrial relevance.
- Work-integrated learning and co-production. <cite id="198a4bb2-3">Industrial doctorates explicitly expand collaboration and render doctorate boundaries “porous,” aligning research with regional industry needs</cite> and facilitating technology transfer and entrepreneurship. <cite id="198a4bb2-4">However, challenges persist: balancing industrial and academic expectations, limited company support for structured planning (Integrated Study Plans), and feedback gaps can undermine outcomes when timelines are tight</cite>.
- Standards, recognition, and incentives. <cite id="198a4bb2-3">Traditional PhD evaluation criteria and resource constraints can be misaligned with industrial doctorates; new indicators and adequate funding are needed to ensure quality and completion</cite>. <cite id="4abf6ba1-0">EPSRC-supported university–industry projects demonstrate sizable gains in employment and turnover for partnered firms six years after project start, relative to comparable firms</cite>, suggesting that when industry sponsorship is present, accelerated or aligned training can enhance economic linkages.

Evidence from fast-track/industrial doctorate models
- Employability and skills. <cite id="198a4bb2-0">Evaluations of UK CASE industrial partnerships report higher employability and broader skillsets among alumni</cite>, consistent with models that embed industrial problems, milestones, and co-supervision into a shorter timeline. <cite id="a5e35afd-2">Women engineering PhDs, for example, show permeable transitions across sectors, highlighting the need for transferable skills and early-career placements to diversify destinations</cite>.
- Commercialization and innovation spillovers. <cite id="198a4bb2-3">Industrial doctorates expand collaboration, aligning doctoral research with societal and entrepreneurial needs; they are increasingly common but vary in policy, selection, supervision, and skills focus</cite>. <cite id="4abf6ba1-0">At the ecosystem level, Innovate UK and EPSRC-supported projects yield measurable employment and turnover growth for firms six years post-funding, with especially large effects for small firms</cite>, consistent with the thesis that tighter university–industry alignment strengthens downstream productivity.
- Supervision and feasibility constraints. <cite id="198a4bb2-4">Companies and academics often struggle to coordinate goals and feedback within industrial co-production; without robust processes and support, compression risks underdelivering on outcomes</cite>. <cite id="a5e35afd-4">Cross-national data from China show many engineering professors enter academia directly after PhD with little to no industry experience, and hiring often expects at least a year of industry experience—underscoring the importance of practical exposure</cite>. In contrast, U.S. university hiring practices frequently favor candidates with prior industry experience, signaling to programs that experiential components are critical to sectoral mobility.

Country and policy cases
- UK policy and flows. The UK has long emphasized enabling PhD graduates to “flow freely between academia, business and other sectors,” with research councils redesigning training to support diverse careers. <cite id="4abf6ba1-1">National strategy explicitly targets varied and diverse careers for PhD holders</cite>, and empirical work finds that connecting PhD students with industry during candidacy improves transitions into non-academic research roles. <cite id="4abf6ba1-2">Moreover, across disciplines, preparing students for non-academic employment and involving non-academic partners in training is essential; traditional assessment alone offers limited formative value for non-academic roles</cite>. These conditions are compatible with a 3-year track if it embeds CASE-style co-supervision, industry projects, and career coaching.
- Germany and France: industry-embedded habilitation reforms. While detailed causal evaluations vary by national context, <cite id="198a4bb2-3">the broader literature documents how industrial doctorates and habilitation-like reforms reshape university–industry knowledge matching, expand collaborative supervision, and encourage commercialization roles</cite>. The risk of weakening links arises if reforms preserve long, decoupled timelines or reduce time for embedded company rotations and joint problem definition; strengthening occurs when the habilitation/3-year restructuring compels earlier, deeper co-production with firms.

Cross-national contrasts on industry experience and implications for a 3-year track
- Demand for industry-relevant experience. <cite id="a5e35afd-4">In the U.S., a majority of engineering faculty had private-sector employment before or immediately after their PhD, and top universities often require at least a year of industry experience for new faculty</cite>. In China, <cite id="a5e35afd-4">only about 5% of engineering faculty had industry experience after their PhD, reflecting “three academic stages,” which weakens translation and commercialization linkages</cite>. For a 3-year track to strengthen productive-sector ties, it should mandate or incentivize industry immersion (paid research, internships, CASE projects) and credential recognition by employers.
- Mobility and sectoral permeability. <cite id="a5e35afd-2">Engineering PhD alumni show nonlinear, cross-sector transitions, with early roles (e.g., postdoc or industry) shaping later faculty attainment</cite>. A shorter degree can accelerate movement into industry roles, but it must also provide scaffolds for later academic mobility (e.g., publishable outputs, transferable methods).

- Likely to strengthen:
  - If paired with industrial co-supervision and joint problem selection, with milestones tied to employer KPIs and deliverables. <cite id="198a4bb2-0">Co-guidance by academic and industry mentors improves employability and skill breadth</cite>.
  - If it embeds structured work-integrated learning (paid internships, company projects, entrepreneurship curricula) and employer networking, increasing time-to-practice and knowledge transfer. <cite id="198a4bb2-3">Industrial doctorates expand matching between regions’ industries and doctoral projects, improving porous boundaries and commercialization pathways</cite>.
  - If it is supported by funding and assessment reforms that recognize practice-ready outputs, not only a thesis viva. <cite id="4abf6ba1-2">Traditional viva-based assessment has limited formative value for non-academic roles; competency-based and demonstrable impact indicators are recommended</cite>. <cite id="4abf6ba1-0">Firms partnered with university research consortia exhibit large employment and turnover gains over six years</cite>.

  - If it compresses breadth, mentoring, and time for alignment with employer needs without adequate resources or standards, leading to lower quality and weak employer recognition. <cite id="198a4bb2-4">Industry partners often lack feedback mechanisms and struggle with academic–industrial expectation mismatches</cite>, and <cite id="198a4bb2-3">traditional evaluation criteria and funding gaps hinder completion and legitimacy</cite>.

Actionable design principles for a 3-year track
- Embed industrial co-supervision and deliverables. <cite id="198a4bb2-0">Co-guide projects with an industry mentor; integrate company KPIs, milestones, and recruitment pipelines into the curriculum</cite>.
- Require work-integrated learning. <cite id="4abf6ba1-2">Mandate multi-month industry placements or CASE projects before dissertation defense to ensure practical relevance and transferable skills</cite> and <cite id="a5e35afd-2">map early-career roles to later sectoral destinations</cite>.
- Align assessment with practice-ready outputs. <cite id="4abf6ba1-2">Adopt competency frameworks and recognize artifacts like prototypes, patents, standards, or startup roles alongside a thesis</cite>, consistent with <cite id="198a4bb2-3">new indicators tailored to collaborative, innovation-oriented doctorates</cite>.
- Provide ecosystem scaffolds: funding and consortia. <cite id="4abf6ba1-0">Leverage university–industry funding programs (e.g., EPSRC/Innovate UK) that have demonstrated employment and turnover gains for partnered firms</cite>; <cite id="198a4bb2-3">reduce institutional barriers and resource gaps that currently impede industrial doctorates</cite>.
- Protect equity and quality. <cite id="198a4bb2-4">Mitigate supervisory and communication challenges via structured plans (Integrated Study Plans), clear expectations, and protected time for co-production</cite>. <cite id="4abf6ba1-4">Ensure inclusivity for early-career researchers via mentoring, workshops, and attention to life-course timing</cite>.

Bottom line
A three-year doctoral track can strengthen links to the productive sector by accelerating time-to-practice, intensifying work-integrated learning, and institutionalizing industrial co-supervision and sponsorship—with evidence of improved employability, broader skills, and measurable firm-level employment and productivity gains when such alignment is present. <cite id="198a4bb2-0">Industrial CASE models show higher employability and broader skills under co-guidance</cite> and <cite id="4abf6ba1-0">firm-level studies show large employment and turnover gains for companies engaged with university research consortia</cite>. However, shortening duration without redesign risks weakening sectoral linkages by compressing breadth, mentoring, and employer-facing validation; success hinges on compensating resources, standards, and assessment reforms that recognize practice-ready competencies and facilitate seamless university–industry collaboration. <cite id="198a4bb2-3">Industrial doctorates succeed when standards and funding are adapted and when collaboration and skills development are explicitly aligned across sectors</cite>, while <cite id="a5e35afd-4">persistent deficits in industry experience before or after the PhD undermine mobility and commercialization in systems that do not embed experiential training</cite>. In sum, “3 years” by itself is not sufficient; “3 years with industry depth” is the condition under which linkages to the productive sector strengthen.

Title: Knowledge or science-based economy? The employment of UK PhD graduates in research roles beyond academia
Snippet: As part of the global trend to high participation systems of higher education (Marginson 2016), the number of PhDs awarded by universities has risen substantially in recent decades (Sarrico 2022). While rates of expansion and labour market conditions vary by country, in most national systems a majority of PhD graduates eventually occupy non-academic employment (Hayter and Parker 2019;OECD 2021). These developments align with an international political consensus over the ascendency of knowledge-based economies, in which research, development and a highly-skilled workforce are forecast to underpin future prosperity (Hancock, Hughes, and Walsh 2017). Within this vision, PhD graduates are framed as human capital of the highest value: prized for their expertise, research training and the potential to broker knowledge transfer between academia, private and public sectors (Hancock 2019;Kyvik and Bruen Olsen 2012;Maheu et al. 2014). 

The UK shares this outlook, having introduced policies and investment to expand doctoral education and broaden skills training to prepare PhD graduates for diverse careers for over two decades (since Roberts 2002). Such is the perceived importance of building research capacity for economic growth and security, the UK government recently declared its ambition to become a 'science and technology superpower' (DSIT 2023). This national strategy places a particular emphasis on enabling PhD graduates to forge 'varied and diverse careers' and 'flow freely between academia, business and other sectors' (DBEIS 2021, 2). 

Beyond the political rhetoric, there is a significant absence of data on the labour market outcomes of PhD graduates amid changing political and economic circumstances. In the UK, understanding of PhD graduates who occupy non-academic careers is severely limitedboth in terms of international standards of knowledge, and in relation to available research on first degree graduates (Hancock, Wakeling, and Chubb 2019). There is a distinct opaqueness surrounding PhD graduates who undertake research employment beyond academia (Hancock 2021). The assumption that PhD graduates working across 'academia, business and other sectors' have comparable and meaningful opportunities to apply their research training has not previously been explored at scale in the UK context. 

This article seeks to address this omission by examining the absorption of UK PhD graduates into research employment beyond academia, and considering how entry into non-academic research roles varies by academic and demographic characteristics.

The balance depends on redesign—not just duration—so that the degree remains recognized by employers and universities while producing earlier entry-to-practice, richer internships/collaborations, and clearer career scaffolding for non-academic roles. <cite id="a5e35afd-0">Recent reviews emphasize that doctoral education must better align with labor-market realities and support diverse sectoral careers, especially beyond academia</cite> <cite id="a5e35afd-3">as tenure-track and federal research roles have shrunk, programs have been called out to systematically prepare students for industry, government, and national labs</cite> <cite id="198a4bb2-3">and industrial doctorates are reshaping knowledge flows across university–industry–government interfaces</cite>.

- Time to practice and market responsiveness. A three-year doctoral track can strengthen links to the productive sector by accelerating time-to-practice, intensifying work-integrated learning, and institutionalizing industrial co-supervision and sponsorship—with evidence of improved employability, broader skills, and measurable firm-level employment and productivity gains when such alignment is present. <cite id="198a4bb2-0">Industrial CASE models show higher employability and broader skills under co-guidance</cite> and <cite id="4abf6ba1-0">firm-level studies show large employment and turnover gains for companies engaged with university research consortia</cite>. Title: Hires-PhD: a transversal skills framework for diversifying PhD employability
Snippet: This study aims to enhance the industrial employability of PhD graduates through the development of the HIRES-PhD framework, an abbreviation of High Impact Research and Employability Skills for the PhD. It identifies and categorizes essential transversal skills. Using a systematic literature review and thematic analysis, we screened 828 papers and selected 39 relevant studies to compile a database of 236 transversal skills. These skills were organized into 16 categories and further distilled into four overarching themes. The HIRES-PhD Framework is compared with traditional models like DOTS, USEM, and MCPHE, as well as recent European initiatives such as DocTalent4EU and OUTDOC. This comparison highlights the framework’s unique focus on doctoral training and industrial employability, unlike traditional models which often target broader educational contexts. Our findings emphasize the importance of a holistic approach to transversal skills training, tailored specifically to the needs of PhD graduates. The HIRES-PhD Framework serves as a comprehensive, data-driven tool for designing PhD programmes that align with industry demands, ensuring that doctoral training is relevant and effective in enhancing employability. In conclusion, the HIRES-PhD Framework significantly contributes to the improvement of doctoral education by providing a structured approach to transversal skills development, thus bridging the gap between academic training and industrial needs. This framework is a valuable resource for policymakers, educators, researchers, and employers aiming to optimize PhD programmes for better employment outcomes.

Title: Towards a Holistic Doctoral Supervision in Africa: An Input-Output Approach
Snippet: The definition of "doctorate" or "doctorateness" is still debated among scholars (Fulgence, 2019;Kálmán et al., 2022;Ngulube, 2021;Poole, 2015;Yazdani & Shokooh, 2018). While there are numerous publications focusing on supervision models, the approach to PhD supervision support receives less attention from researchers (Kálmán et al., 2022;Ngulube, 2021). Further literature is needed to establish robust modes of doctoral supervision ion. Most studies show that doctoral education supervision still predominantly follows a conventional approach (Fetene & Tamrat, 2021;Fulgence, 2019). As the world moves towards a knowledge-based economy, it is crucial to keep up with the evolving demands (Ngulube, 2021). Combining the study's findings with the supervision support model, a doctorate education support model (inputs, transformational process, industry, feedback loop, output) was developed (Figure 1). This study argues in favor of the input-output doctoral supervision support paradigm. Industrial doctorates offer greater employment opportunities compared to traditional ones, promoting candidates with diverse skills who understand both academic and business expectations (Kálmán et al., 2022). Therefore, there is a need to revisit the current doctoral supervision model so that the product can serve both academics and industry. 

Industry supervisors, alongside primary academic supervisors, are responsible for ensuring the scientific quality and successful completion of doctoral projects (Kálmán et al., 2022;Van't Land, 2011).

Title: Knowledge or science-based economy? The employment of UK PhD graduates in research roles beyond academia
Snippet: As part of the global trend to high participation systems of higher education (Marginson 2016), the number of PhDs awarded by universities has risen substantially in recent decades (Sarrico 2022). While rates of expansion and labour market conditions vary by country, in most national systems a majority of PhD graduates eventually occupy non-academic employment (Hayter and Parker 2019;OECD 2021). These developments align with an international political consensus over the ascendency of knowledge-based economies, in which research, development and a highly-skilled workforce are forecast to underpin future prosperity (Hancock, Hughes, and Walsh 2017). Within this vision, PhD graduates are framed as human capital of the highest value: prized for their expertise, research training and the potential to broker knowledge transfer between academia, private and public sectors (Hancock 2019;Kyvik and Bruen Olsen 2012;Maheu et al. 2014). 

The UK shares this outlook, having introduced policies and investment to expand doctoral education and broaden skills training to prepare PhD graduates for diverse careers for over two decades (since Roberts 2002). Such is the perceived importance of building research capacity for economic growth and security, the UK government recently declared its ambition to become a 'science and technology superpower' (DSIT 2023). This national strategy places a particular emphasis on enabling PhD graduates to forge 'varied and diverse careers' and 'flow freely between academia, business and other sectors' (DBEIS 2021, 2). 

Beyond the political rhetoric, there is a significant absence of data on the labour market outcomes of PhD graduates amid changing political and economic circumstances. In the UK, understanding of PhD graduates who occupy non-academic careers is severely limitedboth in terms of international standards of knowledge, and in relation to available research on first degree graduates (Hancock, Wakeling, and Chubb 2019). There is a distinct opaqueness surrounding PhD graduates who undertake research employment beyond academia (Hancock 2021). The assumption that PhD graduates working across 'academia, business and other sectors' have comparable and meaningful opportunities to apply their research training has not previously been explored at scale in the UK context. 

This article seeks to address this omission by examining the absorption of UK PhD graduates into research employment beyond academia, and considering how entry into non-academic research roles varies by academic and demographic characteristics.

Snippet: The highest uptake of the UK's doctoral loans is among non-science scholars (Bennett 2020), but the data presented here suggest that the outcomes for these graduates are furthest removed from the promises of knowledge economy policy. The problem with a universal approach to doctoral expansion is that it conceals differentiations in supply and demand by doctoral subject and institution. PhD holders do not have equal access to high-skilled research employment in the wider economy. 

Across all doctoral programmes, the importance of preparing students for non-academic employment and involving non-academic partners in doctoral training is clear. Connecting PhD students with industry partners during the doctoral candidacy forms the basis of a more harmonious transition into non-academic research employment, for both graduates and employers (Germain-Alamartine et al. 2021;Hottenrott and Lawson 2017;Marini 2022). These reflections lend support to the current strategy of the UK research councils and universities, but more should be done, particularly in relation to informing prospective and current PhD students of likely career outcomes and the prospects for research employment. Following the lead of countries in East Asia, it may be timely to reconsider current methods of assessing the knowledge and competencies required by PhD holders. The longstanding practice of preparing a written thesis and undertaking a viva voce examination may be of limited formative value to PhD holders entering non-academic employment (Shin, Postiglione, and Ho 2018). 

There are many forms of value to undertaking doctoral study (Bryan and Guccione 2018), but the economic imperatives of growth and prosperity continue to dominate the drive for expansion globally. From the limited data available, PhD employment trajectories in the UK emerge as highly differentiated by doctoral institution and subject. Future research endeavours should prioritise the collection of richer longitudinal data on the employment of PhD graduates beyond academia, in order to explore the spectrum of research occupations and assess the research component of roles held by arts, humanities and social sciences graduates in particular. Since the UK is a leading destination for doctoral study internationally, expanding the analysis to include UK PhD holders of all nationalities would be further insightful to understanding employment patterns in an age of global science (Marginson 2022b;Mathies and Cantwell 2022).

While rates of expansion and labour market conditions vary by country, in most national systems a majority of PhD graduates eventually occupy non-academic employment (Hayter and Parker 2019;OECD 2021). These developments align with an international political consensus over the ascendency of knowledge-based economies, in which research, development and a highly-skilled workforce are forecast to underpin future prosperity (Hancock, Hughes, and Walsh 2017). Within this vision, PhD graduates are framed as human capital of the highest value: prized for their expertise, research training and the potential to broker knowledge transfer between academia, private and public sectors (Hancock 2019;Kyvik and Bruen Olsen 2012;Maheu et al. 2014). 

The UK shares this outlook, having introduced policies and investment to expand doctoral education and broaden skills training to prepare PhD graduates for diverse careers for over two decades (since Roberts 2002). Such is the perceived importance of building research capacity for economic growth and security, the UK government recently declared its ambition to become a 'science and technology superpower' (DSIT 2023). This national strategy places a particular emphasis on enabling PhD graduates to forge 'varied and diverse careers' and 'flow freely between academia, business and other sectors' (DBEIS 2021, 2). 

Beyond the political rhetoric, there is a significant absence of data on the labour market outcomes of PhD graduates amid changing political and economic circumstances. In the UK, understanding of PhD graduates who occupy non-academic careers is severely limitedboth in terms of international standards of knowledge, and in relation to available research on first degree graduates (Hancock, Wakeling, and Chubb 2019). There is a distinct opaqueness surrounding PhD graduates who undertake research employment beyond academia (Hancock 2021). The assumption that PhD graduates working across 'academia, business and other sectors' have comparable and meaningful opportunities to apply their research training has not previously been explored at scale in the UK context. 

This article seeks to address this omission by examining the absorption of UK PhD graduates into research employment beyond academia, and considering how entry into non-academic research roles varies by academic and demographic characteristics.

PhD holders do not have equal access to high-skilled research employment in the wider economy. 

Across all doctoral programmes, the importance of preparing students for non-academic employment and involving non-academic partners in doctoral training is clear.
